Pregnancy

When does a baby’s brain develop during pregnancy?

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Your baby’s brain starts forming in the earliest weeks of pregnancy and keeps developing long after birth. There is no single month when intelligence is created, and no supplement, playlist or prenatal activity can guarantee a particular level of ability.

Brain development begins before a pregnancy is obvious

There is no month when intelligence suddenly appears. The nervous system starts taking shape very early, and growth, organization and connections continue throughout pregnancy. After birth, development carries on through childhood and adolescence. Prenatal growth creates foundations; it does not set a measurable final intelligence score.

Pregnancy weeks are usually counted from the first day of the last menstrual period, rather than the day of conception. This explains some apparently conflicting timelines. An account of development three weeks after fertilization may describe roughly five weeks of pregnancy. Ask which dating method is being used before comparing week-by-week information.

The developing structures have different jobs

The cerebrum is the large upper part of the brain. Its networks will contribute to sensation, memory, emotions, language, movement and thinking. The cerebellum helps coordinate movement and balance. The brainstem connects with the spinal cord and supports essential automatic functions, including breathing and cardiovascular regulation.

The hypothalamus helps regulate body temperature, hunger, thirst and sleep-related rhythms and links nervous-system signals with hormone control. The pituitary is a hormone-producing gland closely connected to it, with roles that include growth and regulation of other glands.

These are five useful structures to understand, not five equal subdivisions that develop separately and then switch on in sequence. Naming a structure and its later function does not mean the fetus already has the mature ability. For example, the emergence of the cerebral cortex is not evidence of abstract reasoning in the womb.

The first trimester: building the early framework

During early pregnancy, cells destined to form the nervous system organize into a neural plate, then fold into a neural tube. In pregnancy-week descriptions, this process is underway around weeks 5–6. The brain develops from the head end, while the spinal cord develops along the tube. This early period helps explain why folic acid is important before many people know they are pregnant.

As the first trimester progresses, the early brain regions expand and nerve cells develop. Cells communicate through developing networks, and spontaneous movements can become visible on ultrasound before the pregnant person can feel them. Early movements are part of nervous-system development, not deliberate demonstrations of intelligence.

Descriptions sometimes attach one precise week to the first electrical activity or list yawning and stretching as proof of sophisticated brain function. What researchers can detect depends on the method and on how a movement is defined. A scan showing an early movement cannot tell you what the fetus understands, experiences or will be able to do later.

The second trimester: growth and increasing coordination

The middle months bring extensive production, movement and organization of nerve cells, with developing connections between regions. Movement becomes more varied and coordinated. Sensory systems are developing too, although their timing differs and none should be treated as a single test of future learning ability.

Popular descriptions sometimes give an enormous number of new neurons per minute. Such figures are broad research estimates, not a rate that applies to every region, week or pregnancy. They are not measurements your maternity team uses to decide whether your baby is intelligent or developing normally.

The brainstem continues to mature; it is not fully adult-like at the end of the second trimester. Fetal breathing movements are practice movements, while oxygen comes through the placenta. A baby born very early may need substantial support with breathing and other functions, even though the relevant structures are already present.

The third trimester: more connections and a changing surface

The later months are another important period of brain growth. The cortex develops increasingly prominent folds and grooves, and the cerebellum and networks involved in movement and sensation continue to develop. These changes increase complexity, but size alone is not a measure of intelligence.

A statement that brain weight triples is meaningful only when the starting and ending gestations and the measurement are defined. It should not become a target for an individual pregnancy. Ultrasound and any specialist imaging assess particular clinical questions; a parent cannot judge brain growth by the size of the bump or the strength of kicks.

By birth, the brain has many recognizable structures, yet its networks remain immature. Newborn behavior reflects both capacities already present and a long process of development still to come. Birth is a transition into a different environment, not the finish line for the brain.

Sleep, hearing and familiarity are not an intelligence test

Organized patterns of activity and rest become more evident as pregnancy advances. Researchers describe developing sleep states and eye movements, but observing a REM-like pattern does not establish that a fetus dreams in the way an older child or adult does. We cannot ask a fetus to describe an experience, so the limits of the evidence matter.

The American Academy of Pediatrics describes the beginning of hearing internal sounds around 18 weeks and some sounds from outside the body, including a parent’s voice, around 27–29 weeks. These are approximate developmental descriptions, not deadlines for every pregnancy.

Repeated sounds can become familiar. That is different from understanding the meaning of a story, learning a language as a speaking child does, or showing abstract thought. There is no reason to rank babies by whether they seem to move when someone talks. If a usual movement pattern changes, follow maternity advice rather than trying to prove hearing with music.

Nutrition supports development without promising a higher IQ

Folate is needed for new cells. Folic acid taken before pregnancy and during early pregnancy helps prevent certain neural tube defects. CDC recommends 400 micrograms daily for people who can become pregnant; some circumstances require a clinician-prescribed higher dose. This is prevention advice, not a claim that extra tablets produce a more intelligent baby.

If you discovered your pregnancy after the early weeks, start a conversation about the appropriate supplement now rather than assuming you have caused harm. Do not compensate by taking several prenatal products at once. Review what is already in your supplement so that the combined dose is appropriate.

Omega-3 fats, including DHA, contribute to development, and fish can provide these and other nutrients. Choose lower-mercury fish and follow pregnancy food-safety guidance. FDA/EPA guidance recommends two to three servings a week from its lower-mercury “Best Choices” group for pregnant or breastfeeding adults. If you do not eat fish, ask about suitable dietary or supplement options; no food or DHA brand can guarantee an IQ outcome.

Everyday care matters more than a brain-training program

Avoid alcohol and tobacco exposure during pregnancy, and ask for support if changing their use is difficult. Review medicines, supplements and relevant workplace or household exposures with the maternity team. Do not stop an essential prescribed medicine without a plan, because untreated illness can also affect pregnancy.

Suitable activity, rest, nourishing food and help with stress can support your own health. Fresh air or exercise is not a proven way to increase a fetus’s intelligence, and ordinary worry does not mean that you have damaged the brain. Ask for practical help if anxiety, unsafe conditions or access to food and care is a problem.

Talking, singing or reading something meaningful to you can be a pleasant way to connect. You do not need special recordings, a particular language or a scheduled prenatal lesson. Keep listening comfortable; do not turn sound up to make the baby respond. If these activities feel like another chore, it is fine to wait until after birth.

Development continues long after birth

A newborn learns through everyday relationships and experiences: being comforted, hearing voices, seeing faces and gradually exploring the world. Responsive interaction, conversation, play and reading provide opportunities to learn. You do not have to turn each interaction into a performance test.

Brain maturation continues through the teenage years and into young adulthood. NIMH describes important maturation into the mid-to-late twenties, but this is not a universal switch at age 25. Different skills and networks have different trajectories, and learning and adaptation continue across life.

If a scan raises a concern, ask what was actually seen, whether further imaging or specialist advice is needed and what remains uncertain. After birth, use developmental checks and discuss concerns with your child’s clinician. Neither a reassuring prenatal movement nor a single milestone can predict the whole course of a child’s abilities.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Prenatal anatomy, movement and sound responses describe development; they do not measure intelligence.

Early folic acid and suitable pregnancy nutrition support health without guaranteeing cognitive outcomes.

How BeMama can help

Choose a manageable routine for your own care. Talking or singing can be enjoyable bonding, with no schedule or performance target.

When to seek help

Discuss medicines, supplements, exposures and scan findings with your maternity team. Follow its advice promptly if your baby’s usual movements reduce or change.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • The nervous system begins forming early in pregnancy.
  • Brain structures and their mature functions are not the same thing.
  • Development continues in every trimester and after birth.
  • Familiar sounds do not demonstrate language comprehension or abstract thought.
  • Nutrition and care support health without an intelligence guarantee.

Frequently asked questions

In which month does intelligence develop?

There is no single month. Abilities emerge through a long developmental process before and after birth.

Why do two timelines give different weeks?

One may count from conception and another from the last menstrual period, usually about two weeks earlier. Check the dating method.

Are the cerebrum, cerebellum, brainstem, hypothalamus and pituitary five equal brain regions?

No. They are useful structures to discuss, but the pituitary is a closely connected hormone gland and the list is not a set of five equivalent divisions.

Does early movement mean the fetus is thinking deliberately?

No. Spontaneous movement reflects developing nervous-system activity and does not establish conscious reasoning.

Is the brainstem fully mature by the end of the second trimester?

No. It continues maturing, and premature babies may need support with essential functions.

Do fetal eye movements prove dreaming?

No. Sleep-state observations cannot establish the content or existence of a subjective dream experience.

Does recognizing a voice mean understanding language?

No. Familiarity with repeated sounds is different from understanding words or abstract ideas.

Will extra folic acid make my baby more intelligent?

That is not the purpose of folic acid advice. It helps prevent neural tube defects; take the appropriate dose rather than adding extra products.

Do I need to play special music every day?

No. Reading or singing can be enjoyable, but there is no required prenatal teaching routine.

Does the brain stop changing at 25?

No. Some important maturation continues into the twenties, but there is no universal birthday cutoff and learning continues throughout life.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
